nameStory: This whale is named after Frederick W. True, a curator at what is now the Smithsonian Institution who studied marine mammals in the late 1800s and early 1900s. True was one of the pioneering scientists who helped us understand the mysterious world of beaked whales, a group so elusive that many species weren't discovered until the 20th century.
description: True's beaked whale is a medium-sized whale that belongs to one of the ocean's most mysterious mammal families. These deep-diving whales have elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies and distinctive beak-like snouts that give them their name. Adult males can reach about 17 feet long, while females grow slightly larger at around 18 feet. They're incredibly rare to spot, spending most of their lives in deep ocean waters far from shore.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized whale with a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body about the length of a large motorboat, distinctive long beak-like snout, and relatively small dorsal fin set far back on the body

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Dark grayish-brown to blackish upper body with lighter gray or whitish underside, often with linear scars from squid tentacles creating pale streaks across the skin

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely elusive, surfacing briefly with just the top of head and small dorsal fin visible before diving for 20-30 minutes to hunt deep-sea squid

idTips.label: Head Features
idTips.description: Adult males have two small teeth that protrude from the lower jaw like tiny tusks, visible when the mouth is closed, while females' teeth remain hidden

habitat: True's beaked whales live in deep ocean waters of the North Atlantic, typically found far offshore in areas where the continental shelf drops off into abyssal depths of 3,000 feet or more. In New England waters, any sighting would likely occur many miles from shore in the deep waters beyond the continental shelf edge.

seasonality.spring: Rarely observed, but any sightings would likely occur during calm weather when deep ocean waters are accessible to researchers.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for any potential whale watching encounters, though sightings remain extraordinarily rare even during optimal ocean conditions.
seasonality.fall: Continued presence in deep Atlantic waters, but approaching winter storms make observations even less likely.
seasonality.winter: Present in deep ocean but virtually impossible to observe due to harsh North Atlantic conditions.

funFact: True's beaked whales are so mysterious that scientists know more about some dinosaurs than these living mammals - the very first True's beaked whale wasn't scientifically described until 1913, and there has been only one confirmed sighting in all of New England waters!
confusionNotes: Could potentially be confused with other beaked whale species, but True's beaked whale is distinguished by the male's small, forward-pointing teeth and the species' preference for very deep offshore waters. Remember: if you see a beaked whale in New England waters at all, it's an extraordinary event worth reporting to marine mammal researchers.
contextualKnowledge: The entire beaked whale family represents one of the least understood groups of large mammals on Earth, with some species known only from specimens that have washed ashore. True's beaked whale exemplifies this mystery - despite being larger than many land mammals we see daily, it remains virtually unknown to science.
compareHints: True's beaked whale is the only Mesoplodon species recorded in New England waters, making it impossible to confuse with close relatives in the region. Compared to other beaked whale families that might occur in the North Atlantic, True's beaked whale is medium-sized with a more pronounced beak and the distinctive small teeth visible in adult males. Unlike the larger northern bottlenose whale, True's beaked whale has a more slender build and darker coloration.
